articleHeadline: H1N1, dengue put city on fever watch
articleSummary:
- Ahmedabad, India, is under a fever watch as late-July rains and hot, humid weather drive infections. H1N1 influenza is rising alongside dengue, malaria, chikungunya, typhoid, jaundice, and gastroenteritis. About six of every ten cases are viral fevers, with influenza in children marked by high fever plus headache, body aches or sore throat; several cases occur in family clusters. Most illnesses are not severe, and hospitalisation remains low. Residents are urged to clear standing water, avoid self-medication, and seek care if symptoms persist beyond two days; mosquito protection and hygiene are emphasized. - Ahmedabad city’s health department, Aug 1–9, reported 113 gastroenteritis cases (diarrhoea/vomiting), 46 typhoid, and 17 jaundice; 13 simple malaria and 1 falciparum malaria; 19 dengue and 1 chikungunya in the nine-day window. From Jan 1 to Aug 9, totals reach 3,669 gastroenteritis, 1,247 typhoid, 469 jaundice; dengue 246; malaria 188 (including 20 falciparum); chikungunya 4. Water testing covered 16,536 residual chlorine samples, with six showing no residual chlorine; 2,453 bacteriological samples were collected, with 10 declared unfit for consumption. Data come from Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation’s city-wide surveillance and reflect persistent enteric and vector-borne disease activity during this period. The release notes ongoing monitoring and public health measures.

The surge coincides with the monsoon season; health authorities say hospitals are prepared, with separate wards and private rooms for H1N1 and dengue. Common H1N1 symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, body aches, and fatigue. While many experience a typical flu, older adults, pregnant women, young children, and those with diabetes or chronic heart or lung disease face higher risk of severe illness. Antibiotics do not treat H1N1; antiviral medicines may be used depending on severity and risk factors. - As of 2026-08-11, H1N1 influenza activity in Delhi-NCR worries pediatricians: 25–30 schoolchildren present daily with flu-like symptoms at the OPD. Among those tested, 3–4 are positive for H1N1. Because symptoms closely resemble a routine viral flu, waiting for laboratory confirmation can result in critical delays in treatment, according to Dr Amit Gupta, Senior Consultant-Pediatrician and Neonatologist at Motherhood Hospitals. The report underscores the need for timely recognition and management of H1N1 in children amid the current surge.

One year before transplantation he had a positive C-ANCA (1:40). In 2025 he was treated for active pulmonary tuberculosis (RIPE regimen), during which rifampicin lowered tacrolimus levels, prompting dose adjustments in his triple immunosuppressive therapy (tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, prednisone). Post-transplant, he developed fever, allograft dysfunction, proteinuria, hematuria, and rising C-ANCA; renal biopsy showed pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis consistent with recurrent ANCA-associated vasculitis. Authors highlight that infection or its treatment can paradoxically trigger AAV reactivation in transplant recipients and stress close immunosuppression monitoring, individualized management, and multidisciplinary decision-making to balance infection control with autoimmunity treatment.

articleSummary: As of 11 August 2026, dengue management in Brazil advises extreme caution with dental care during the acute phase. Oral dengue manifestations occur in up to 30% of cases, commonly spontaneous gingival bleeding, and can include palatal red or purplish spots, ulcers, lip crusts, and a metallic taste; distinguish from chronic gingivitis by abrupt bleeding with fever and body aches. Recovery of coagulation takes 1–2 weeks; resume invasive treatment 14–21 days after symptom end, with a complete blood count. In emergencies, use safe analgesics (paracetamol or dipyrone); avoid NSAIDs and aspirin. Interdisciplinary, conservative management prioritizes safety.

articleHeadline: Impact of Climate Change on Africa's Malaria Map.
articleSummary: Nature’s late-July study shows climate change reshapes Africa’s malaria map. While anomalous warming generally boosts malaria, effects vary by region. Rising temperatures are projected to increase malaria risk in southern Africa and East Africa’s highlands, but may reduce transmission in current hotspots that become too hot for mosquitoes. In major West African countries—Nigeria, Burkina Faso, and Mali—cases could decline by about 5%. In very hot Sahel nations Niger, the Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, and Somalia, malaria could disappear as conditions become inhospitable for vectors. Cooler, historically non-endemic areas such as the southern parts of Africa and East Africa’s highlands face higher risk, with around 5% increases reported in the Ethiopian Highlands, Kenya, Burundi, and similar rises in Angola, Zambia, and northeastern South Africa. By 2100, malaria risk could reach 20% in the Rift Valley and southern coastal Africa. Limiting warming to 2C could avert roughly five cases per 1,000 children in southern Africa; adaptation and sustained health funding remain essential.

articleHeadline: Understanding Hantavirus: Jambi Residents Urged to Beware of Symptoms, Sources and Its Spread.
articleSummary: Hantavirus in Jambi Province, Indonesia: Residents urged to beware of symptoms, sources and spread. Rodents such as rats and mice carry hantavirus, which can cause severe kidney and lung disease. The virus is shed in rodent droppings, urine, and saliva; main human transmission occurs when contaminated dust is inhaled or via bites. Dry-cleaning of rodent-infested spaces—especially warehouses or old buildings—can aerosolize particles, so dry sweeping is strongly discouraged. Human-to-human transmission is considered very rare. The term hantavirus originated after the Hantan River in Korea, though awareness has existed long before. At-risk groups include workers cleaning old warehouses, farmers in plantations, and construction workers in aging structures. Prevention emphasizes preventing rodent access and applying PHBS (Clean and Healthy Living Habits).

articleSummary: Davao City records 34 confirmed human rabies deaths from 2021 to 2026, per the City Veterinarian's Office (CVO). Deaths are linked to gaps in responsible pet ownership, delayed vaccination, and failure to seek prompt medical care after animal bites. Preventive measures include responsible ownership, annual vaccination of dogs and cats, immediate wound washing with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, prompt medical attention, completion of Anti-Rabies Vaccine (ARV) and Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) when indicated, and reporting suspected rabid animals. Animal-side data show 95 rabies-positive animals in CY2025–2026 (66 in 2025, 29 in 2026 so far) and 179 lab-confirmed cases 2021–2026, led by Talomo (67), Tugbok (34), Buhangin (22). Vaccination drives: 127,503 (2021), 116,540 (2022), 146,095 (2023), 156,817 (2024), 164,125 (2025); 99,436 vaccinated in 2026 to date, led by Talomo (31,437), Buhangin (12,931), Toril (10,840). In Feb 2026, two Marilog children (ages 2 and 4) died from bites by unvaccinated animals, prompting renewed calls for responsible ownership and immediate care.

articleHeadline: When the rain comes, dengue season follows: 8 things to know
articleSummary: Philippines dengue activity remains a year-round public health concern even as cases decline. The Department of Health reports 50,727 dengue cases from January to May 2026, a 56% decrease from the same period last year, but the rainy season continues to raise Aedes mosquito breeding risk in homes and communities. Dengue is transmitted by Aedes, with symptoms typically appearing 4–10 days after infection and lasting 2–7 days: high fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pains, nausea, vomiting, rash, and fatigue. Warning signs of severe dengue include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, rapid breathing, restlessness, pale skin, or extreme weakness—seek medical attention early. Hydration and avoiding NSAIDs; paracetamol for fever unless advised. DoH’s enhanced 4S strategy—Search and destroy breeding sites, Self-protection, Seek early consultation, and Support fogging only during outbreaks—requires community effort; Manila Doctors Hospital is cited as a local option for evaluation.

articleHeadline: Africa steps up its fight against malaria with millions of doses of a vaccine that can save lives - HSB NOTICIAS.
articleSummary: RTS,S/AS01 became the first WHO-recommended malaria vaccine, with pilots starting in 2019 in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi to evaluate real-world use. By October 2023, >6 million doses had been administered to >2 million children, underpinning a 2021 WHO recommendation for broader deployment. This evidence-supported expansion across Africa was complemented by the addition of a second vaccine, R21/Matrix-M, to increase supply. Malaria, caused by Plasmodium falciparum and transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, remains a major child-health threat in Africa. RTS,S/AS01 targets the circumsporozoite protein to reduce disease risk and severe malaria as part of an integrated approach with insecticide-treated nets, vector control, and prompt diagnosis/treatment. The four-dose regimen begins around five months of age, presenting logistical challenges for health systems to ensure completion. Reported outcomes include about a 13% reduction in all-cause mortality among eligible children and fewer severe malaria cases and hospitalizations.
